extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent agents, and inventors drafting U.S. patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for drafting U.S. patent specifications and claims that work for examiners, litigators, and PTAB review; covers structure, figures-first workflow, claim strategy, and disclosure depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Three Audiences for a Patent Application
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent specification is read by (1) the examiner, who decides whether to allow it; (2) a future district court judge or jury, who decides claim construction and infringement; and (3) a future PTAB panel, who decides validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting choices that satisfy one audience may hurt another. The first draft should be examiner-friendly; later drafts must be litigation-friendly. Balance language and structure to serve initial prosecution while preserving litigation strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brick-by-Brick Description
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the invention as a sequence of components, each with a reference number that ties to the figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walk the reader through (a) what each component is, (b) what it does, (c) what alternatives exist, and (d) how it interacts with neighboring components. The 'bricks' become the building blocks for claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three Independent Claims, Twenty Total
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO filing fee includes three independent claims and twenty total claims. Use them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft three independent claims of varying scope plus seventeen dependent claims that systematically narrow. This gives negotiating leverage with the examiner and creates a more robust claim portfolio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method, System, Apparatus - File All Three
rubrics_metrics.description: For a software-related invention, file parallel sets: a method claim (what the system does), a system/apparatus claim (a processor + memory + instructions), and a computer-readable medium claim (instructions stored on a medium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim type reaches different infringers and survives different invalidity attacks; include all applicable statutory categories to maximize enforcement and defensive options.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Drawing-First Workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with the figures and draft the specification around them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For mechanical inventions include (a) an exploded view, (b) an assembled perspective view, (c) a cross-section, (d) a flowchart of operation. For software include (a) a system architecture diagram, (b) a data flow diagram, (c) a flowchart of the key algorithm, (d) a screen mockup if user-facing. Use figures to anchor reference numbers and the brick-by-brick description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Differentiation as a Drafting Tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dependent claims deliberately to affect the interpretation of independent claims via claim differentiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claim 2 adds 'wherein the widget is metal,' that creates a presumption that claim 1 covers non-metal widgets too. Use dependent claims to broaden or shape the construction of independent claims by negative implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'Best Mode' Requirement Still Exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the AIA removed best-mode failure as a basis for invalidity, the requirement to disclose the best mode under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) still technically exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More importantly, failing to disclose your best mode means a competitor can patent it on top of your patent. Disclose everything — include the best mode in the specification to avoid giving others room to patent the preferred embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting in Layers
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the specification in multiple layers to serve different needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer 1: paragraphs that read like a textbook for a POSITA. Layer 2: paragraphs that recite the elements of each claim, almost word-for-word, so every claim term has clear antecedent support. Layer 3: paragraphs that describe alternatives, ranges, and equivalents. All three layers belong in the spec to support prosecution and later litigation/analysis.
